en: To deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something; to not vote
hook: ABS-TAIN: to keep your ABS, you abstain from sweets.
story: Abstain. To deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something, or to choose not to vote. Every Ramadan, Farhan's grandfather abstains from food and water from dawn to sunset, even in the April heat. This year Farhan, aged twelve, tried a full fast too. At the sunset azan, the family broke their fast with dates and cold sharbat. Farhan drank slowly, proud that he had managed to abstain all day. Abs means away, and tain means hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away. So, what verb means to hold back on purpose? ... Abstain.

gre.s: Although he enjoyed rich food, the athlete chose to ____ from sweets for the entire season, convinced that discipline would sharpen his game.
gre.clue: convinced that discipline would sharpen his game

example: Three council members abstained in the vote on the new bus routes, saying they needed more time to study the plan.

en: Anxiety or fear that something bad will happen; also, understanding or arrest
hook: APPREHENSION: feeling like you're about to be APPREHENDED (arrested).
story: Apprehension. Anxiety or fear that something bad will happen. The night before her viva at Dhaka University, Mitu lay awake under the slow ceiling fan. She kept picturing the examiners frowning and her voice cracking on the first question. By morning her hands were cold and her stomach was tight with apprehension. Then the first examiner smiled kindly, and her apprehension melted away. The trick: to apprehend a thief is to seize him, and apprehension is the dread that seizes you before trouble arrives. So, what word names the uneasy fear that something will go wrong? ... Apprehension.

gre.s: Although the villagers greeted the new dam with ____, fearing floods and lost farmland, their worries proved unfounded when the first monsoon passed without incident.
gre.clue: fearing floods and lost farmland

example: Despite her apprehension about flying for the first time, Nanu smiled through the whole journey from Dhaka to Jeddah.

en: Suggesting that things will go well; a good sign
hook: AUSPICIOUS: AUSPICES were bird signs Romans read for good luck.
story: Auspicious. Suggesting that things will go well; a good sign. On the first morning of his small tea stall near Chittagong College, Kamal was nervous. Before he had even boiled the milk, a professor stopped, [gasp] ordered ten cups for his whole department, and promised to come back every day. Kamal [laugh] grinned with relief. What an auspicious start. In ancient Rome, a priest called an auspex watched the flight of birds for signs, and good signs were called auspicious. So, what word describes a beginning that promises success? ... Auspicious.

gre.s: The campaign's opening day was hardly ____: the candidate's car broke down on the way, and a sudden storm emptied the rally ground before she could speak.
gre.clue: the candidate's car broke down on the way

example: Three wide-margin wins in its first week were an auspicious beginning for the newly formed university cricket team.

en: To send someone away officially as punishment; to get rid of
hook: BANISH: make them VANISH.
story: Banish. To send someone away officially as punishment; also, to get rid of something. On the train to Rajshahi, Tanvir reached a sad page in his history book. After the revolt of eighteen fifty-seven, the British banished the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, to Rangoon. The old poet wrote of longing for Delhi and never saw it again. Tanvir closed the book and watched the fields for a long time. Banish rhymes with vanish: to banish someone is to make them vanish from the land. So, what verb means to send someone out of their country as punishment? ... Banish.

gre.s: Determined to ____ every trace of the old regime, the new government renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks.
gre.clue: renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks

example: A brisk walk along the river and a cup of strong tea were usually enough to banish Rokeya's morning gloom.

en: Cruelly uncaring about other people's pain
hook: CALLOUS: hardened like a CALLUS on the skin.
story: Callous. Cruelly uncaring about other people's pain. On a hot afternoon in Mirpur, an old rickshaw puller slipped and fell under a heavy load of rice sacks. A man in a shiny car honked at him to move, then drove around without a glance. A student named Joya ran to help him up shaking with anger at such callous behaviour. The trick: a callus is hard skin on a working hand, and a callous heart has grown just as hard, so others' pain cannot reach it. So, what word describes someone who does not care when others suffer? ... Callous.

gre.s: The official's ____ response to the flood victims, whom he dismissed as careless people who deserved their fate, provoked outrage across the country.
gre.clue: dismissed as careless people who deserved their fate

example: The company's callous decision to fire injured workers by text message, with no compensation, sparked protests outside its headquarters.

en: A sharp split separating two opposite ideas or groups
hook: DI-CHOTOMY: cutting in two (di = two, tomy = cut).
story: Dichotomy. A sharp split separating two opposite ideas or groups. From the window of a Gulshan tower, Sara could see both shores of the lake at once. On one side stood glass buildings and rooftop gardens. On the other lay the tin roofs of Korail, packed so tightly they almost touched. The dichotomy between the two shores stayed with her all evening. Dicho means in two, and tomy means cutting: a dichotomy cuts something cleanly in two. A false dichotomy offers only two choices when more exist. So, what word names a sharp split between two opposite sides? ... Dichotomy.

gre.s: The author rejects the traditional ____ between reason and emotion, arguing that the two are deeply intertwined in every decision.
gre.clue: arguing that the two are deeply intertwined

example: Many medical students feel a dichotomy between the science they learn in lectures and the folk remedies their grandparents swear by.

en: Extremely or unusually small
hook: DIMINUTIVE: DIMINISHED in size.
story: Diminutive. Extremely or unusually small. Priya's headmistress was barely taller than the girls in class six. Yet when she walked into the morning assembly and raised one small hand, eight hundred students fell silent at once. Priya, standing in the back row, [chuckle] always smiled at the sight. That diminutive woman ran the whole school like a general, and everyone loved her for it. Diminutive shares its root with diminish, to make smaller, so a diminutive thing looks as if it has been diminished. So, what word describes someone or something unusually tiny? ... Diminutive.

gre.s: Despite his ____ stature, the jockey controlled the enormous stallion with remarkable strength and confidence.
gre.clue: controlled the enormous stallion

example: The diminutive hummingbird beats its wings so fast that they blur into a faint hum.

en: To bend out of normal shape; to present facts falsely
hook: DIS-TORT: TWISTED (torque) out of shape.
story: Distort. To bend something out of its normal shape, or to present facts falsely. At the Shishu Park funfair, Arif [laugh] grinned at himself in a curved mirror that made him tall and wobbly. A newspaper printed only half of his uncle's speech, and suddenly the kind man seemed to be insulting farmers. The mirror had distorted his body; the paper had distorted his uncle's words. Tort comes from the Latin for twist, as in torture: to distort is to twist out of shape. So, what verb means to twist facts until they become false? ... Distort.

gre.s: By quoting only fragments of her speech, the article managed to ____ her position, making her appear to support a policy she had criticized.
gre.clue: making her appear to support a policy she had criticized

example: Cheap speakers distort the bass, so the drums on the recording sounded like someone banging on a tin box.

en: Gradually becoming smaller or fewer
hook: DWINDLE: shrinking like a candle's WICK.
story: Dwindling. Gradually becoming smaller or fewer. When Imran moved into a Dhaka hostel, his father gave him twelve thousand taka to last the month. Books, rickshaw fares and late-night tea each took their share. By the third week the bundle in his drawer was dwindling fast, and he was eating rice and egg every night. Each time he counted it, [sigh] the dwindling pile felt thinner. Dwindling rhymes with kindling: like a small fire of kindling, it burns lower and lower until little is left. So, what word describes a supply that is slowly shrinking away? ... Dwindling.

gre.s: Conservationists warn that the species' ____ population, now fewer than two hundred animals, may not survive another decade.
gre.clue: now fewer than two hundred animals

example: With dwindling daylight and no torch, the hikers gave up on reaching the waterfall and turned back toward the village.

en: Believing that a select group is superior and deserves special treatment
hook: ELITIST: thinks only the ELITE matter.
story: Elitist. Believing that a select group is superior and deserves special treatment. Ishita joined a debate club where the senior members listened only to students from three expensive English-medium schools. When a brilliant girl from a village college stood up to speak, two of them rolled their eyes. Ishita felt ashamed, and she left the club the next week. Its attitude was openly elitist. The trick: an elitist believes only the elite matter, and the opposite is egalitarian, believing everyone is equal. So, what word describes someone who thinks a privileged few deserve special treatment? ... Elitist.

gre.s: The university's admissions policy was attacked as ____, since it effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring.
gre.clue: effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring

example: Some readers dismiss literary prizes as elitist, arguing that the judges reward books ordinary people find dull.

en: Deeply upsetting and painful to live through or hear about
hook: HARROWING: like a HARROW (farm tool) tearing through your heart.
story: Harrowing. Deeply upsetting and painful to live through or hear about. Anika's grandfather rarely spoke about nineteen seventy-one. One winter evening he told the family how he hid for nine days in a flooded jute field, listening to soldiers search the village, with only raw rice to eat. No one moved. Anika held his hand as he finished his harrowing story. A harrow is a farm tool that tears through the soil, and a harrowing experience tears through the heart in the same way. So, what word describes an experience so painful it is hard even to hear? ... Harrowing.

gre.s: Survivors of the shipwreck gave ____ accounts of the night they spent clinging to wreckage in freezing water, many of them watching companions drown beside them.
gre.clue: watching companions drown beside them

example: The film's harrowing portrayal of the 1943 famine left many viewers sitting in silence long after the credits rolled.

en: Consisting of many different kinds of things
hook: HETERO = different, GENE = kind. Different kinds mixed.
story: Heterogeneous. Consisting of many different kinds of things. Sara's GRE coaching batch in Farmgate was a surprising mix: a young doctor, a banker, a fresh graduate, a fifty-year-old engineer and a cricket coach from Khulna. They had different ages, accents and dreams. Every discussion went somewhere new, and Sara looked forward to each class. Such a heterogeneous group taught her more than any textbook. Hetero means other or different, and gen means kind: different kinds mixed together. Its opposite is homogeneous, all of one kind. So, what word describes a group made of many different kinds? ... Heterogeneous.

gre.s: Far from being uniform, the region's population is remarkably ____, comprising dozens of languages, religions, and ethnic groups.
gre.clue: Far from being uniform

example: Granite looks smooth from a distance, but up close it is heterogeneous, speckled with grains of quartz, feldspar and mica.

en: Too dense to get through, or too difficult to grasp
hook: IM-PENETRABLE: can't PENETRATE it.
story: Impenetrable. Too dense to get through, or too difficult to understand. On a boat in the Sundarbans, Rafi stared at the wall of mangrove roots along the bank, twisted so tightly that not even a monkey could squeeze through. "Impenetrable," the guide said. Back in his hostel, Rafi opened a philosophy book so full of jargon that it felt just as impenetrable. Im means not, so impenetrable means it cannot be penetrated, whether it is a forest or an idea. So, what word describes a forest you cannot enter, or a text you cannot understand? ... Impenetrable.

gre.s: Although the theorist claimed to be writing for a general audience, her prose proved virtually ____, so dense with jargon that even specialists struggled to follow it.
gre.clue: even specialists struggled to follow it

example: Thick fog made the mountain pass impenetrable, and the convoy waited until noon for it to lift.

en: Fixed so deeply in a person or culture that it rarely changes
hook: INGRAINED: deep IN the GRAIN of the wood.
story: Ingrained. Fixed so deeply in a person or culture it rarely changes. Rahim left his village twenty years ago for a glass office in Banani. Yet he still wakes before dawn without an alarm, still takes off his shoes at every door, and still stands up when an elder enters the room. His colleagues tease him gently, but these habits are ingrained. Picture a stain soaked deep into the grain of a wooden table: no scrubbing can remove what is in the grain. So, what word describes a habit fixed so deep it rarely changes? ... Ingrained.

gre.s: Prejudices that are ____ in a culture rarely vanish with the passage of a single law; they persist for generations, handed down quietly from parents to children.
gre.clue: they persist for generations

example: Checking his phone first thing every morning was so ingrained that Imran did it even on holiday at the beach.

en: A temporary period of calm; to calm or send to sleep
hook: LULL: a LULLABY puts you to sleep.
story: Lull. A temporary period of calm; as a verb, to calm someone or send them to sleep. All afternoon a storm pounded the tin roof of Joya's house in Barisal. Then, near sunset, the wind dropped and the rain stopped. Her father hurried out to tie up the goats. In that short lull, Joya's mother sat on the bed, [sigh] humming softly, and lulled the baby to sleep. Lull is hidden inside lullaby, the soft song that lulls a child to sleep. So, what word names a short, quiet pause in a storm? ... Lull.

gre.s: After weeks of relentless fighting, a brief ____ allowed aid workers to deliver food to the city, though the shelling resumed within two days.
gre.clue: allowed aid workers to deliver food

example: The gentle rocking of the launch on the Meghna soon lulled the children to sleep.

en: Over almost as soon as it begins
hook: MOMENTARY: lasts a MOMENT.
story: Momentary. Over almost as soon as it begins. The teacher held up the results sheet in front of class ten and paused. In that momentary silence, Ishita could hear the ceiling fan creak and her own heart pounding. Then the teacher read out her name. Ishita [gasp] covered her mouth as the room burst into cheers. Her fear had been momentary; her joy lasted all week. Momentary lasts only a moment, so do not confuse it with momentous, which means hugely important. So, what word describes a silence that lasts only a moment? ... Momentary.

gre.s: The pilot's ____ lapse in concentration lasted only a second, but it was long enough to put the plane dangerously off course.
gre.clue: lasted only a second

example: A momentary gap in the clouds let the astronomers photograph the comet before the sky closed over again.

en: Just beginning to exist; showing signs of future potential
hook: NASCENT: newly born (natal), like a newborn.
story: Nascent. Just beginning to exist, and showing signs of future potential. Sumaiya and her friend started selling handmade jute bags from a tiny room in Mohammadpur, with one sewing machine and a Facebook page. In the first month they sold only eleven bags, but every buyer came back for more. Their business was nascent, small and fragile, yet clearly growing. Sumaiya packed each order herself, as carefully as if it were a gift. Nascent comes from the Latin for being born, the same root as native. So, what word describes something newly born and just starting to grow? ... Nascent.

gre.s: Investors hesitated to fund the ____ industry, since it was still in its infancy and no company had yet proved it could earn a profit.
gre.clue: still in its infancy

example: Bangladesh's nascent space programme reached a milestone in 2018, when the country's first communications satellite was launched.

en: Moving quickly and easily; also quick in thinking
hook: NIMBLE: as quick as a NIMBLE squirrel.
story: Nimble. Moving quickly and easily; also quick in thinking. In the crowded Gulistan market, a young porter carried a basket of vegetables on his head, weaving between rickshaws, buses and shoppers without bumping a single person. Tanvir watched from a tea stall, amazed by those nimble feet. That evening, at a university debate, he saw a girl answer every tricky question in a flash; her mind was just as nimble. Remember the old rhyme, Jack be nimble, Jack be quick: nimble simply means quick and light. So, what word describes someone light and quick on their feet? ... Nimble.

gre.s: Though the old pianist's body had grown frail, his fingers remained astonishingly ____, racing through the most difficult passages without a single error.
gre.clue: racing through the most difficult passages

example: A nimble debater, Faria turned every attack from her opponent into a point in her own favour.

en: To leave out or fail to include
hook: OMIT: OMISSION, something left out.
story: Omit. To leave out or fail to include. Kamal filled in his visa form late at night and submitted it, [sigh] relieved to be done. A week later it came back. He had omitted his middle name, which was printed clearly in his passport. One missing word, and the whole application stopped. Now he reads every form twice, so he never omits a thing. Omit sounds a little like oh, missed it, which is exactly what you say when you omit something. The noun is omission. So, what verb means to leave something out? ... Omit.

gre.s: In order to keep the report brief, the authors chose to ____ several minor findings, mentioning only those results directly relevant to the policy debate.
gre.clue: mentioning only those results directly relevant to the policy debate

example: The recipe card omitted the salt, so Babli's first batch of pitha tasted strangely flat.

en: Grabbing any chance for gain, even against one's principles
hook: OPPORTUNISTIC: grabs every OPPORTUNITY, ethical or not.
story: Opportunistic. Grabbing any chance for gain, even against one's principles. When a rumour spread that salt would run out, worried families in Old Dhaka rushed to the shops. A few traders hid their stock and sold it at five times the usual price. They had not started the rumour, but they hurried to profit from other people's fear. Their neighbours never fully trusted them again after such opportunistic greed. An opportunist grabs every opportunity, fair or unfair. So, what word describes someone who seizes any chance for profit, whatever it costs their principles? ... Opportunistic.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the politician's sudden embrace of environmental causes as ____, noting that he had opposed every green initiative until polls showed voters cared about them.
gre.clue: until polls showed voters cared about them

example: Opportunistic scammers posted fake relief appeals within hours of the cyclone, hoping to steal donations meant for survivors.

en: Bizarrely strange or unusual
hook: OUT-LANDISH: from an OUTside LAND, totally foreign and weird.
story: Outlandish. Bizarrely strange or unusual. On a bus to Gazipur, a seller stood up with a bottle of yellow oil. It could cure toothache, baldness, back pain and even bad luck, he said, all for fifty taka. Farhan's grandmother [chuckle] leaned over and whispered that if it really worked, the seller would surely have a full head of hair himself. Such outlandish claims never fooled her. Outlandish once meant foreign, from an outside land, so anything outlandish seems to come from somewhere very strange. So, what word describes a claim so bizarre that it is hard to believe? ... Outlandish.

gre.s: The theory that the pyramids were built by visitors from another planet is so ____ that serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it.
gre.clue: serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it

example: The student's outlandish excuse, that a monkey had stolen her assignment from the rooftop, turned out to be completely true.

en: To spread widely; to breed or reproduce
hook: PROPAGATE: like PROPAGANDA spreading everywhere.
story: Propagate. To spread widely, or to breed and multiply. Every monsoon, Ishita's mother cut small stems from her rose bushes in Dhanmondi, planted them in clay pots, and gave the new plants to neighbours. Within a few years, roses bloomed on half the balconies of the lane. She had propagated them, one cutting at a time. Ideas propagate the same way, passed from hand to hand. The word shares a root with propaganda, which is something spread on purpose. So, what verb means to breed something and spread it widely? ... Propagate.

gre.s: Rather than suppress the rumour, the agency's clumsy denial served only to ____ it, as thousands of users shared the statement with mocking comments.
gre.clue: as thousands of users shared the statement

example: Early printing presses helped propagate the reformers' ideas across Europe far faster than handwritten copies ever could.

en: Intended to correct or improve something, especially weak skills
hook: REMEDIAL: provides a REMEDY.
story: Remedial. Intended to correct or improve something, especially weak skills. After his first GRE practice test, Shuvo stared at his quant score and felt his face go hot. He had forgotten fractions and basic geometry since school. So he joined a remedial maths class in Farmgate every evening, rebuilding the basics one step at a time. Eight weeks later his score jumped, and he called his mother from the street to tell her. Remedial comes from remedy: a remedial class is a remedy for weak skills. So, what word describes lessons meant to fix what you never learned properly? ... Remedial.

gre.s: Because so many incoming students lacked basic writing skills, the university introduced ____ courses designed to correct these deficiencies before regular classes began.
gre.clue: designed to correct these deficiencies

example: After the audit, the bank took remedial steps, retraining its cashiers and installing software to catch suspicious transfers.

en: Good at finding clever ways to solve problems
hook: RESOURCEFUL: full of RESOURCES in your mind.
story: Resourceful. Good at finding clever ways to solve problems. A storm cut the power in Tania's village an hour before her online university interview, and her phone was nearly dead. She ran to a neighbour's house, charged it from their small solar panel, then climbed onto the cowshed roof for a better signal. She logged in, [sigh] with two minutes to spare. Later the interviewer said that was exactly the kind of resourceful student they wanted. A resourceful person is full of resources, especially inner ones like wit and courage. So, what word describes someone who always finds a way? ... Resourceful.

gre.s: Stranded without tools when their car broke down in the desert, the ____ travelers repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings and reached the next town by nightfall.
gre.clue: repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings

example: Resourceful as ever, Grandmother turned the leftover rice into crispy fritters that the children liked better than dinner.

en: Excessively indulging one's own desires
hook: SELF-INDULGENT: INDULGING the SELF too much.
story: Self-indulgent. Excessively indulging one's own desires. After his exams ended, Zayan bought a whole box of roshogolla and ate every single one alone on the rooftop. Then he slept until noon, skipped his cousin's birthday, and spent the evening watching films. By night he felt sick and a little guilty. One self-indulgent day is fine, his mother said gently, but a self-indulgent life is not. To indulge is to give in to a desire, so to be self-indulgent is to give in to your own. So, what word describes giving in too much to your own wants? ... Self-indulgent.

gre.s: The editor urged the novelist to cut her lengthy digressions about her own childhood, which, however satisfying to write, struck readers as ____ and irrelevant to the plot.
gre.clue: however satisfying to write

example: The singer's self-indulgent twenty-minute guitar solo emptied half the auditorium before the final song.

en: Knowing what to say so that you do not upset others
hook: TACT: a gentle TACTILE touch with words.
story: Tact. Knowing what to say so that you do not upset others. Nadia's aunt served a biryani that was far too salty, and the table went quiet. Nadia sipped some water and said, "The meat is so tender, Khala. You must teach me how you cook it." It was true, and her aunt beamed with pride. That was tact: honest kindness without a sharp edge. The word comes from the Latin for touch, as in tactile, so tact is a gentle touch with words. So, what word names the skill of speaking without hurting feelings? ... Tact.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ in handling the dispute, defusing tensions without insulting either party, won her praise from both governments.
gre.clue: defusing tensions without insulting either party

example: Breaking the news of the cancelled trip to forty excited schoolchildren required more tact than the young teacher possessed.

en: To offer lower prices than a competitor; to weaken or undermine
bn: কম দামে বিক্রি করা; দুর্বল করা
hook: UNDER-CUT: CUT the price UNDER theirs, or cut UNDER the foundation.
story: Undercut. To offer lower prices than a competitor; also, to weaken or undermine. When a big grocery app arrived in Mohammadpur with cheaper rice and lentils, Rahim's small corner shop lost half its customers. The app had undercut him. But Rahim knew every family by name, gave credit when times were hard, and remembered which child liked which biscuit. Slowly, people returned. No app could undercut that trust. Picture cutting under a wall until it falls, or cutting your price under someone else's. So, what verb means to sell more cheaply than a rival, or to weaken them? ... Undercut.

gre.s: The witness's repeated contradictions served only to ____ the credibility of the defense, which had built its entire case on his reliability.
gre.clue: repeated contradictions

example: Cheap imported toys undercut the craftsmen of Sonargaon, who could not match prices made possible by mass production.

en: Hard to control and inclined to go its own way
hook: WAYWARD: going AWAY from the right path.
story: Wayward. Hard to control and inclined to go its own way. During the Shakrain kite festival on the rooftops of Old Dhaka, Mahin's kite caught a gust and refused to obey him. It swooped, spun and drifted toward the neighbour's water tank. Mahin [gasp] tugged the string, but the wayward kite went wherever it pleased. His grandfather [chuckle] said Mahin had been just as wayward as a little boy. Wayward is a shortened form of awayward, turned away from the path you are meant to follow. So, what word describes something that refuses to be controlled and goes its own way? ... Wayward.

gre.s: The novel follows a ____ teenager who drifts from one reckless adventure to another before finally finding purpose.
gre.clue: drifts from one reckless adventure to another

example: A wayward kite drifted across the rooftops of Old Dhaka during the Shakrain festival before tangling in a coconut tree.

en: Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses
hook: WHIMSICAL: full of WHIMS.
story: Whimsical. Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses. Lamia's art teacher painted the classroom ceiling with flying fish, umbrellas growing like flowers, and a cat riding a rickshaw through the clouds. The students loved every corner of it. One rainy morning she whimsically cancelled the drawing test and took them all to sketch boats by the river. A whim is a sudden fancy, so a whimsical person is full of whims. So, what word describes art or a mood that is playful, fanciful and full of sudden impulses? ... Whimsical.

gre.s: The architect's otherwise sober design included one ____ touch: a staircase painted to look like a row of giant piano keys.
gre.clue: otherwise sober design

example: The picture book is full of whimsical touches, such as an elephant postman who delivers letters with his trunk.

en: Intentional; stubbornly determined to do as one wants
hook: WILL-FUL: full of your own WILL.
story: Willful. Intentional; also, stubbornly determined to do as one wants. At her cousin's wedding, Rumana's three-year-old nephew refused to wear shoes. Sandals were offered, then a chocolate, then his grandmother's gentle pleading. He sat on the floor, folded his arms, and went barefoot all evening. Everyone [chuckle] agreed he was the most willful guest there. In law, willful damage is damage done on purpose, not by accident. The trick: willful means full of will, your own will and nothing else. So, what word describes someone stubbornly set on getting their own way? ... Willful.

gre.s: The court ruled that the company's failure to report the leak was not an innocent oversight but a ____ deception, carried out with full knowledge of the risks.
gre.clue: not an innocent oversight

example: Smashing the bus shelter during the protest was a willful act, the magistrate said, and the fine would reflect that.
